title: Rakos_Malware_Investigation_d5c
description: Investigate the Rakos malware, a Linux backdoor that performs brute force SSH login attempts to compromise devices and servers with weak passwords.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Unix/Linux system administration
Familiarity with systemd services and timers
outcomes: Usage of systemctl for service management
Investigation of systemd timers for persistence mechanisms
Analysis of system logs for lateral movement indicators
Identification of suspicious services and their configurations

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The Rakos malware is a Linux backdoor that performs brute force SSH login attempts to compromise devices and servers with weak passwords. It aims to assemble a list of unsecured devices to create a botnet. The malware is written in Go and typically compressed with UPX. It has capabilities for updating its configuration and upgrading itself. During this investigation, you will encounter service names such as `javaxxx.service` and other system-related flags.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have access to the target host with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. From this host, you can investigate the system and any connected hosts. Enter the word 'start' to proceed to the next level.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content: Investigate the target host for any unauthorized or suspicious services running. What is the name of the suspicious service running on the target host?
levels.solution: Check the running services and look for any that seem unusual or unauthorized. The suspicious service is named `javaxxx.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Consider what types of services might be running on a Linux system and how you can list them.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use systemctl to list all running services and look for any that seem unusual or unauthorized.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious service name starts with 'java' and ends with '.service'.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot. What is the persistence mechanism used by the suspicious service?
levels.solution: Investigate systemd services and timers to find how the service is started automatically. The persistence mechanism is a systemd timer named `javaxxx.timer`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Think about how services can be configured to start automatically on a Linux system.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use systemctl to list all timers and look for any associated with the suspicious service.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The persistence mechanism is a systemd timer named `javaxxx.timer`.

levels.title: Identify Lateral Movement
levels.content: Identify file transfers or remote execution used to move between hosts. What is the service name, filename, or destination host used for lateral movement?
levels.solution: Check the system logs and network connections for evidence of lateral movement. The service name used for lateral movement is `javaxxx.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Consider how malware might move laterally between hosts on a network.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use journalctl to check the logs of the javaxxx.service for evidence of lateral movement. The correct command is journalctl -u javaxxx.service.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The service name used for lateral movement is `javaxxx.service`.
